chapters.title: Moses recalls the journey and the refusal to enter

parts.text: In the fortieth year, Moses begins explaining God’s law to Israel east of Jordan. He recalls the command to leave Horeb and possess the land promised to their fathers. Because the people had multiplied beyond what he could govern alone, wise and respected men were appointed as judges. They were instructed to hear fairly, show no partiality, and bring difficult cases to Moses.

Moses recounts the journey to Kadesh-barnea, the sending of spies, and Israel’s fearful refusal to enter despite God’s past care. God declared that the unbelieving generation would not inherit the land, except Caleb and Joshua. When the people then attempted to fight against his command, they were defeated. Their later weeping did not reverse that judgment.

chapters.title: The wilderness years and the defeat of Sihon

parts.text: Moses recalls Israel’s long journey around Mount Seir. God forbade them to seize land belonging to Esau, Moab, or Ammon because he had assigned those territories to their peoples. Israel was to buy necessary food and water. Historical notes describe earlier inhabitants displaced in those lands. Thirty-eight years passed from Kadesh-barnea until the disobedient fighting generation had died.

God then directed Israel against Sihon king of Heshbon. Moses requested peaceful passage, offering to buy provisions, but Sihon refused and came out to battle. The LORD gave him and his territory into Israel’s hands. Israel took his cities and spoil while leaving the forbidden Ammonite territory untouched, following the boundaries of God’s command.

chapters.title: Eastern victories and Moses’ unfulfilled request

parts.text: Moses recounts the defeat of Og king of Bashan, including the capture of his many fortified cities. The conquered territories of Sihon and Og are described and distributed to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Their fighting men must cross Jordan with their brethren, leaving families and livestock behind, until the other tribes receive the rest and inheritance God has promised.

Moses reminds Joshua that the LORD who defeated these kings will also defeat the kingdoms ahead. He then recalls pleading to cross Jordan and see the good land. God refuses further discussion of that request but allows him to view the country from Pisgah. Moses must charge, strengthen, and encourage Joshua, who will lead Israel into its inheritance.

chapters.title: Remember God’s covenant and reject idols

parts.text: Moses urges Israel to keep God’s statutes without adding or taking away. Their experience at Baal-peor shows the danger of disobedience. God’s nearness and righteous laws should display Israel’s wisdom to other nations. They must remember Horeb and teach their children: they heard God’s voice but saw no manner of similitude. Therefore they must not make images of people, animals, or heavenly bodies for worship.

Moses warns that idolatry will bring destruction and scattering, yet those who seek God wholeheartedly in distress will find him, for he will not forget his covenant. Israel’s deliverance and hearing of God’s voice demonstrate his uniqueness. Moses sets apart three eastern cities of refuge, and the chapter introduces the law he gives in the plains east of Jordan.

chapters.title: The covenant commandments repeated

parts.text: Moses calls Israel to hear, learn, and obey the covenant made at Horeb. He repeats the commandments: worship only the LORD, reject images, honor his name, keep the sabbath, honor parents, and abstain from killing, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting. Sabbath rest extends to servants, strangers, and animals, and Israel must remember its own bondage and God’s deliverance from Egypt.

God spoke these words from the fire and wrote them on stone tablets. Terrified, the people asked Moses to receive further commands and relay them. God approved their words and expressed his desire that they always fear him and obey. Moses urges them not to turn aside, so they may live and prosper in the land they will possess.

chapters.title: Love the LORD and teach his words

parts.text: Moses calls Israel to fear the LORD and keep his commands throughout their generations. The LORD their God is one LORD, and they must love him with all their heart, soul, and might. His words must remain in their hearts, be taught diligently to children, and shape daily conversation and household life. When they receive cities, houses, wells, and vineyards they did not build, they must not forget their deliverer.

Israel must serve the LORD alone, refuse other gods, and not test him as at Massah. Obedience will help them possess the promised land. When children ask about the laws, parents must recount slavery in Egypt, God’s mighty deliverance, and his purpose in giving commands for their continuing good and preservation.

chapters.title: A chosen people must refuse Canaan’s gods

parts.text: Moses commands Israel to destroy the nations God delivers into their hands, make no covenant with them, and avoid marriages that would turn their children to other gods. Their altars and images must be destroyed. Israel is holy and chosen, not because it is the largest nation, but because God loves it and keeps his oath to the fathers. He is faithful to those who love him and judges those who hate him.

If Israel obeys, God promises fruitfulness, health, and victory. They must not fear stronger nations but remember what he did to Egypt. The inhabitants will be removed gradually. Israel must reject their idols completely, including the precious metals on them, and must not bring an accursed object into its house.

chapters.title: Remember the wilderness when prosperity comes

parts.text: Moses reminds Israel that the wilderness journey humbled and tested them. God allowed hunger and supplied manna to teach that life depends on every word proceeding from his mouth. Their clothing did not wear out, and he disciplined them as a father disciplines a son. They are entering a good land with abundant water, crops, minerals, and food, for which they must bless him.

Prosperity brings a warning: full houses, growing herds, and increasing wealth must not cause Israel to forget the LORD who delivered and sustained them. They must not credit their own strength for their possessions, because God gives the power to obtain wealth in keeping with his covenant. Forgetting him and following other gods will bring destruction like that of the nations before them.

chapters.title: Israel’s inheritance is not earned by righteousness

parts.text: Moses warns Israel not to think victory over stronger nations proves its own righteousness. God drives those nations out because of their wickedness and to fulfill his oath to the patriarchs. Israel itself has been stubborn and rebellious. Moses recalls receiving the covenant tablets after forty days on Horeb, only to be told that the people had quickly corrupted themselves by making an image.

He recounts breaking the tablets at the sight of the golden calf, destroying it, and interceding for the people and Aaron. Other rebellions at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and Kadesh-barnea confirm the pattern. Moses’ prayer appealed to God’s ownership of Israel, his promises to the fathers, and the honor of his name among the nations, rather than Israel’s merit.

chapters.title: Renewed tablets and the obedience God requires

parts.text: Moses recounts making new stone tablets and an ark at God’s command. God writes the same covenant words on the tablets, which Moses places in the ark. The account also recalls Aaron’s death, Eleazar’s succession, and Levi’s appointment to carry the ark, minister, and bless in the LORD’s name. Moses’ further intercession is heard, and God commands the journey onward.

What God requires is wholehearted fear, love, service, and obedience. Though heaven and earth belong to him, he chose Israel’s fathers and their descendants. They must put away stubbornness. God shows no partiality, takes no bribes, and defends the fatherless, widow, and stranger. Israel must likewise love the stranger, remember Egypt, and cleave to the LORD who has multiplied them.

chapters.title: Blessing and curse set before Israel

parts.text: Moses appeals to the generation that has seen God’s mighty acts, discipline, and judgments, including Egypt’s defeat and the fate of Dathan and Abiram. They must love and obey him to possess the land and prolong their days there. Unlike Egypt, this land depends upon rain from heaven and remains under the LORD’s care. Obedience brings seasonal rain and provision; turning to other gods brings closed skies and loss of the land.

God’s words must be held in the heart, taught to children, and displayed in daily life. Faithful obedience will bring victory over stronger nations. Moses sets blessing and curse before Israel, directing that the blessing be pronounced on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal after they cross Jordan.

chapters.title: Worship where God places his name

parts.text: Israel must destroy the nations’ places of worship, altars, pillars, groves, and images. They must bring sacrifices, tithes, firstfruits, and vowed gifts to the place the LORD chooses for his name, rejoicing there with their households and remembering the Levite. Their settled worship must follow God’s command rather than each person doing what seems right in his own eyes.

Ordinary meat may be eaten in their towns, including by clean and unclean people, but blood must be poured out rather than consumed. Sacred offerings still belong at God’s chosen place. Israel must not imitate the nations’ worship or inquire how to copy it, since those peoples even burn their children to their gods. Nothing may be added to or removed from God’s command.

chapters.title: Reject every invitation to worship other gods

parts.text: A prophet or dreamer must be rejected if he urges worship of other gods, even when a predicted sign occurs. Such a test reveals whether Israel loves the LORD wholeheartedly. The offender is to die for promoting rebellion against their deliverer. Even a close relative or beloved friend who secretly entices someone to idolatry must not be shielded from judgment.

If a city is reported to have turned to other gods through corrupt leaders, Israel must investigate thoroughly before acting. If the report is established, the city and its inhabitants are devoted to destruction, and none of its spoil may be retained. Obedience in this matter turns away God’s fierce anger and preserves the mercy promised to the fathers.

chapters.title: A holy people’s food and tithes

parts.text: Because Israel belongs to the LORD as his holy people, they must not adopt forbidden mourning practices involving cutting themselves or shaving for the dead. Moses distinguishes clean and unclean animals, fish, and birds, repeating the rules about divided hooves, chewing the cud, and fins and scales. They must not eat an animal that dies naturally or boil a kid in its mother’s milk.

A yearly tithe of produce is eaten before the LORD at his chosen place, teaching Israel to fear him. If the journey is too far, its value may be carried as money and used to provide the feast there. The Levite must not be neglected. Every third year, tithes are stored locally for Levites, strangers, fatherless children, and widows to eat and be satisfied.

chapters.title: Release debts and deal generously with the poor

parts.text: Every seventh year brings a release from debts owed by fellow Israelites. God promises blessing for obedience, yet commands openhanded care when a brother is poor. The approaching year of release must not become an excuse to refuse a needed loan. Israel must give willingly, remembering that poor people will remain in the land and that generosity receives God’s blessing.

Hebrew servants are released after six years and must be sent away with generous provisions, recalling Israel’s own slavery and redemption. A servant who freely chooses to remain may have his ear pierced as a lasting sign. Firstborn males of herd and flock are set apart for the LORD; blemished firstlings may be eaten locally, but their blood must not be consumed.

chapters.title: Three pilgrimage feasts and impartial justice

parts.text: Moses commands Israel to keep passover in the month Abib, remembering the night God brought them from Egypt. Sacrifice takes place at the LORD’s chosen location, and seven days of unleavened bread recall the hurried departure. The feast of weeks follows the harvest count and includes a voluntary offering. The feast of tabernacles celebrates gathered produce. Households rejoice with servants, Levites, strangers, fatherless children, and widows, and every male appears before God three times yearly with a gift.

Judges and officers must be appointed in Israel’s towns. They must pursue justice without partiality or bribery, since gifts corrupt judgment. Moses also forbids placing a grove beside the LORD’s altar or setting up an image, which God hates.

chapters.title: Justice, central judgments, and the king’s limits

parts.text: Israel must not sacrifice blemished animals. Reports of idolatry require diligent investigation, and execution requires two or three witnesses, whose hands initiate the sentence. Difficult cases are brought to the priests and judge at the LORD’s chosen place. Their decision must be followed; presumptuous refusal carries death so that the people will hear and fear.

If Israel asks for a king, he must be chosen by the LORD and be an Israelite. He must not multiply horses, return the people to Egypt for them, multiply wives, or greatly accumulate silver and gold. He must write and continually read a copy of the law, learning humility and obedience rather than lifting himself above his brethren.

chapters.title: Priests, forbidden divination, and the promised prophet

parts.text: The Levites have no territorial inheritance like the other tribes; the LORD is their inheritance. Priestly portions and firstfruits provide their support, and a Levite who comes to serve at God’s chosen place shares in the appointed food. Israel must reject child sacrifice, divination, witchcraft, familiar spirits, and consultation of the dead, practices for which God drives out the nations.

Moses announces that the LORD will raise a Prophet like him from among Israel’s brethren, answering their earlier request not to hear God’s terrifying voice directly. God will put his words in that Prophet’s mouth and require obedience. A prophet speaking presumptuously or in another god’s name is condemned. A prediction that fails to occur exposes a word the LORD has not spoken.

chapters.title: Refuge, boundaries, and truthful witnesses

parts.text: Israel must establish accessible cities of refuge to protect a person who kills unintentionally from the avenger of blood. Moses illustrates accidental death with an axe head slipping off during woodcutting. If God enlarges their territory as promised and they obey him, additional refuge cities are required. These protections must not shelter deliberate murderers, who are to be handed over for judgment.

Inherited landmarks must not be moved. A single witness cannot establish an offense; two or three are required. When a witness is accused of false testimony, priests and judges must investigate diligently. A proven false witness receives the punishment he intended for the accused. This removes evil and deters others, applying judgment proportionate to the harm intended.

chapters.title: Instructions for warfare

parts.text: When Israel faces a stronger army, it must not fear, because the LORD who brought it from Egypt goes with it. A priest encourages the soldiers before battle. Officers then release men who have a new undedicated house, an unused vineyard, or a betrothed wife, as well as those who are fearful and might discourage others. Captains are appointed over the remaining force.

Distant cities are first offered terms of peace; refusal leads to siege and the prescribed judgment. Different commands apply to the nations in Israel’s inheritance, whose practices must not draw Israel into sin. During a prolonged siege, fruit trees must be preserved for food rather than cut down; non-fruit trees may be used for siegeworks.

chapters.title: Unsolved murder, household duties, and burial

parts.text: When a murdered person is found and the killer is unknown, the nearest city’s elders perform a prescribed ceremony with a heifer and declare their innocence before the priests, asking God to remove bloodguilt. A captive woman taken as a wife must receive time to mourn and be treated according to the law; if later rejected, she must be released rather than sold or treated as merchandise.

A father may not deprive his actual firstborn of the double inheritance because he prefers another wife’s son. A persistently rebellious son is brought by his parents before the city’s elders for judgment. Someone executed and hung on a tree must be buried the same day, so the land is not defiled; the chapter identifies the hanged person as accursed of God.

chapters.title: Neighborly care and laws concerning sexual wrongdoing

parts.text: Israelites must return lost animals and possessions and help a fallen animal rather than ignoring a neighbor’s need. Other commands distinguish men’s and women’s clothing, spare a mother bird when taking young, require a protective roof battlement, and prohibit certain mixtures in sowing, plowing, and clothing. Fringes are required on garments. These laws address responsibility, distinctions, and preventable harm in ordinary life.

The remaining laws concern accusations about a bride’s virginity, adultery, and sexual encounters involving betrothed or unbetrothed women. They distinguish false charges, consensual wrongdoing, and an assault where a woman has no rescuer. Penalties and marriage obligations vary with the circumstances. The chapter closes by forbidding a man to take his father’s wife.

chapters.title: The holy camp and obligations toward others

parts.text: Moses gives restrictions on entry into the congregation, including those concerning Ammon and Moab because of their treatment of Israel and hiring Balaam. Edom and Egypt receive different treatment, and later generations may enter. Israel’s military camp must remain holy: bodily uncleanness requires temporary withdrawal and washing, and waste must be buried outside, because the LORD walks among the camp to deliver them.

A fleeing servant must not be returned to his master or oppressed. Prostitution and its proceeds are excluded from sacred vows. Interest may not be charged to an Israelite brother, and vows must be fulfilled promptly, though making a vow is voluntary. A traveler may eat a neighbor’s grapes or pluck grain by hand, but may not harvest it for storage.

chapters.title: Protection for families, workers, and the vulnerable

parts.text: The law forbids a man to take back a former wife after her intervening marriage ends. A newly married man receives a year free from military or public duties to remain with his wife. Millstones must not be taken as pledges, since they sustain life. Kidnapping an Israelite for enslavement or sale is punishable by death. Israel must heed the priests’ instructions concerning leprosy, remembering Miriam.

A lender must respect the borrower’s home and return a poor person’s needed garment before night. Hired workers must be paid promptly. Individuals are judged for their own sins, and justice for strangers, fatherless children, and widows must not be distorted. Forgotten sheaves, remaining olives, and leftover grapes are reserved for the vulnerable, recalling Israel’s bondage in Egypt.

chapters.title: Fair punishment, family duty, and honest measures

parts.text: Judges must acquit the righteous and condemn the guilty, limiting corporal punishment to forty stripes so a brother is not degraded. An ox must not be muzzled while treading grain. If brothers dwell together and one dies childless, the surviving brother is to marry the widow and preserve the dead brother’s name. Refusal brings a public ceremony of reproach. Another law addresses a woman’s intervention in a fight by seizing a man’s private parts.

Israel must use honest weights and measures rather than different standards for buying and selling. Dishonesty is an abomination to the LORD. Moses also commands Israel to remember Amalek’s attack on the weak at the rear during the exodus and, once settled and at rest, blot out Amalek’s remembrance.

chapters.title: Firstfruits, shared provision, and covenant commitment

parts.text: When Israel possesses the land, each worshiper brings firstfruits to the LORD’s chosen place. The accompanying declaration recalls the father who went down to Egypt, Israel’s growth, Egyptian oppression, and God’s response to their cries. The worshiper acknowledges that God brought them into a land flowing with milk and honey and now presents its first produce with thanksgiving, rejoicing alongside the Levite and stranger.

In the third-year tithe declaration, the giver affirms that the holy portion has been distributed to Levites, strangers, fatherless children, and widows according to God’s command, and asks for blessing. Moses urges wholehearted obedience. Israel acknowledges the LORD as its God, and he acknowledges them as his special, holy people, charged to keep his commandments.

chapters.title: The law written and covenant curses proclaimed

parts.text: Moses and the elders command Israel, after crossing Jordan, to erect plastered stones and write the law plainly upon them. On Mount Ebal they must build an altar of uncut stones, offer burnt and peace offerings, and rejoice before the LORD. Moses and the priests declare that Israel has become the LORD’s people and must obey his commandments.

The tribes are assigned to Mount Gerizim for blessing and Mount Ebal for cursing. The Levites pronounce curses against hidden idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving landmarks, misleading the blind, denying justice to the vulnerable, forbidden sexual relations, secret murder, and bribery to kill the innocent. The people answer Amen to each, including the final curse upon failure to uphold the words of the law.

chapters.title: Blessings for obedience and curses for rebellion

parts.text: If Israel diligently obeys the LORD, blessings will reach every part of life: towns and fields, children, animals, harvests, daily work, and battles. God will establish them as his holy people, provide rain, and give them a position of strength among nations. These promises are tied to following his commandments without turning to other gods.

Disobedience brings corresponding curses and escalating calamities: disease, drought, defeat, oppression, ruined crops, bereavement, and captivity. A foreign nation will besiege their cities so severely that families turn against their own children for food. God will scatter them among peoples where they find fear and no rest. The lengthy warning ends with a reversal of deliverance, including return toward Egypt and an unsuccessful attempt to sell themselves as slaves.

chapters.title: The covenant in Moab and the danger of secret rebellion

parts.text: Moses recalls God’s wonders in Egypt, his provision through forty wilderness years, and victories over Sihon and Og. He urges obedience so Israel may prosper. All stand before the LORD—leaders, men, women, children, and strangers—to enter his covenant and become established as his people. The covenant also concerns those not present, extending responsibility beyond the immediate assembly.

Moses warns against anyone secretly turning to idols while imagining he will escape judgment. Such stubbornness brings the covenant’s curses. Future generations and foreign visitors will ask why the land lies devastated; the answer will be Israel’s abandonment of the LORD’s covenant. The chapter closes by distinguishing secret things belonging to God from revealed things given to Israel and its children for obedience.

chapters.title: Return to God and choose life

parts.text: Moses looks beyond the blessings and curses to Israel remembering God’s words while scattered among the nations. If they return wholeheartedly to the LORD, he will have compassion, gather them, and restore them to their land. He will circumcise their hearts to love him, turn the curses upon their enemies, and rejoice in doing them good as they obey his voice.

The commandment is not inaccessible in heaven or beyond the sea; the word is near, in their mouth and heart, so they may do it. Moses sets life and good, death and evil before them. He calls heaven and earth as witnesses and urges them to choose life by loving the LORD, obeying him, and cleaving to him in the promised land.

chapters.title: Joshua commissioned and the law preserved

parts.text: At 120 years old, Moses announces that he will not cross Jordan. The LORD will go before Israel, and Joshua will lead them. Moses encourages the people and Joshua to be strong, because God will not fail or forsake them. He entrusts the written law to the priests and elders, commanding a public reading every seventh year at tabernacles so adults, children, and strangers learn to fear and obey God.

God summons Moses and Joshua to the tabernacle and foretells Israel’s future apostasy and resulting distress. Moses must teach a song that will testify against them when these things occur. Joshua receives God’s charge to lead. Moses places the law beside the ark as a witness, gathers the leaders, and begins speaking the song to the congregation.

chapters.title: Moses’ song of witness and his final command

parts.text: Moses’ song calls heaven and earth to hear. It praises the LORD as the faithful, just Rock and contrasts his goodness with Israel’s corruption. God found and cared for Israel, carried them like an eagle, and fed them from the land’s abundance. Yet Jeshurun grew prosperous and forsook his Maker, sacrificing to strange gods. The song describes God’s jealous anger and the judgments that follow.

The song exposes the impotence of false gods and declares the LORD’s power to kill and make alive, wound and heal, judge enemies, and show mercy to his people and land. Moses tells Israel to take these words to heart and teach them to their children, for they are their life. God then commands him to ascend Nebo, view Canaan, and die there because of Meribah-Kadesh.

chapters.title: Moses blesses Israel’s tribes

parts.text: Before his death, Moses blesses Israel, recalling the LORD’s glorious appearing and the giving of the law. He prays for Reuben’s survival and Judah’s help, describes Levi’s testing and teaching ministry, and speaks of Benjamin’s security. Joseph receives an expansive blessing of heaven, deep waters, fruitful hills, and strength, with Ephraim and Manasseh pictured in the power of a firstling bullock.

The remaining blessings address Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, describing prosperity, strength, inheritance, and service in varied images. Moses concludes that none is like Israel’s God, who rides upon the heavens to help them. The eternal God is their refuge, his everlasting arms sustain them, and Israel is blessed as a people saved and defended by the LORD.

chapters.title: Moses dies and Joshua succeeds him

parts.text: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He may see it but will not enter. Moses dies in Moab according to the LORD’s word, and God buries him in a valley; no one knows his grave. At 120 years old, his sight and natural strength had not failed. Israel mourns him for thirty days.

Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses laid hands on him, and the people follow him as commanded. The book closes by describing Moses’ unique place among Israel’s prophets: the LORD knew him face to face, and through him performed mighty signs in Egypt and great acts before all Israel.
